young.html: Before he wrote his great story of Aeneas, the Roman poet Virgil wrote about the countryside where he grew up. His first poems, the Eclogues, are songs sung by shepherds as they watch their flocks. His next poem, the Georgics, is about farming: how to plow, when to plant, how to grow grapes and olives, how to care for cows and horses, and how to keep bees.
Virgil loved the country, but he knew farming was hard work. He tells farmers to watch the sky and the animals for signs of the weather, and to do each job at the right time of year.

young.text: Never is rain on us unwarned: either as it gathers in the valley bottoms the crane soars high in flight before it; or the heifer gazing up into the sky snuffs the breeze with wide-opened nostril, or the shrill swallow darts circling about the pond, and the frogs in the mire intone their old complaint.
young.author: Virgil

young.html: Be a weather watcher. For one week, write down the weather each morning and one thing you notice outdoors: the clouds, the wind, how birds fly, how the air smells. Each evening, guess tomorrow’s weather from your signs, then check. Which of your signs worked best? Real forecasters today use instruments and computers, but they began by watching carefully, just as Virgil told farmers to do.

young.cap: Tap a book of the Georgics to see what it is about, or switch to the ten Eclogues.

young.html: In the last book Virgil writes about bees as if a hive were a tiny city, where everyone has a job and all the work is shared.

full.html: Virgil (70–19 BC) came from farm country near Mantua, in northern Italy. The Eclogues, ten short poems published around 39 BC, were his first book. The Georgics, a poem of four books on farming, took him about seven years and was finished around 29 BC. Both were written as Rome came out of civil war, when Octavian (soon to be called Augustus) was taking power. Virgil’s friend and patron Maecenas, a close adviser of Octavian, is named at the start of every book of the Georgics.

The Eclogues follow the Greek poet Theocritus, whose shepherds sang in the hills of Sicily. Virgil’s herdsmen hold singing contests, mourn a lost friend and sing of love. But Roman troubles break in. After the civil war battle of Philippi in 42 BC, farmland in northern Italy was taken to settle veteran soldiers. The first Eclogue opens with two herdsmen: one has been driven from his land, the other allowed to stay.

full.text: Tityrus, thou where thou liest under the covert of spreading beech, broodest on thy slim pipe over the Muse of the woodland: we leave our native borders and pleasant fields; we fly our native land, while thou, Tityrus, at ease in the shade teachest the woods to echo fair Amaryllis.
full.author: Virgil

full.html: The fourth Eclogue is the most famous. It foretells the birth of a child who will bring back the golden age. Who Virgil meant is still debated; the poem is dedicated to his friend Pollio, consul in 40 BC. Later Christian readers, among them the emperor Constantine, read it as a prophecy of Christ, which is one reason Virgil was so honored in the Middle Ages.

full.text: The Georgics: a poem about work

full.name: gb-georgics
full.cap: The four books of the Georgics, and the ten Eclogues.

full.html: Each book of the Georgics takes one part of farming, but the poem is not a manual. It is about how people should live. In Book I Virgil says the god Jupiter made farming hard on purpose, so that people would grow inventive: “toil conquered everything,” in his words labor omnia vicit improbus, hard, unrelenting toil. Book II praises the quiet life of the farmer, far from war and politics.

full.text: Ah too fortunate the husbandmen, did they know their own felicity! on whom far from the clash of arms Earth their most just mistress lavishes from the soil a plenteous sustenance. … Happy he who hath availed to know the causes of things, and hath laid all fears and immitigable Fate and the roar of hungry Acheron under his feet.
full.author: Virgil
full.note: Two passages a few lines apart; the gap is marked …

full.html: “Happy he who hath availed to know the causes of things” is, in Latin, felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas. Many readers think Virgil had in mind Lucretius, whose poem on atoms (the rung before this one) promised freedom from fear through knowing how nature works. Virgil then adds that the farmer who honors the country gods is blessed too.

Book IV describes the hive as a model community: the bees share their homes, work in turns, store food for winter and defend their ruler. Virgil, like all ancient writers, called the ruler of the hive a king; naturalists of the 1600s showed that it is a female, the queen. The book closes with a myth: the beekeeper Aristaeus loses his bees and learns that he must make amends for the death of Eurydice. Inside this story Virgil tells how Orpheus, her husband, went down to the underworld to bring her back, and lost her again by looking back too soon.

Treating the Georgics as a farming textbook. Some of its advice is sound and some is ancient lore that is wrong (for example, the old belief, which Virgil repeats, that a swarm can be born from the body of a dead bullock; bees come from eggs laid by the queen). Roman farmers had real handbooks, by Cato and Varro. Virgil wrote a poem about work, seasons and how to live well.

items: Pastoral poetry: the Eclogues set the pattern for centuries of shepherd poems in many languages, among them Milton’s Lycidas.
The dignity of work: the Georgics made farming a subject for great poetry. Dryden, who translated all of Virgil, called it “the best poem of the best poet.”
Familiar words: “Love conquers all” (omnia vincit Amor) comes from the tenth Eclogue.

deep.html: Rome had been at war with itself, off and on, since before Virgil was born. The Georgics praise Italy and pray for a ruler who will bring peace, and Book I ends with the bad omens around the murder of Julius Caesar in 44 BC and a world turned upside down: “so many wars, so many faces of crime.” An ancient life of Virgil says he read the finished poem aloud to Octavian in 29 BC, over four days, with Maecenas taking over when the poet’s voice grew tired.

items: Is hard work a curse, or a gift that makes us grow? Virgil seems to say both.
Is the quiet country life happier than the life of a city, or of fame? Or is that a dream of people who do not farm?
What can a community of animals, like bees, teach people? Where does the comparison break down?

deep.html: Virgil’s Aeneid, the next rung, turned from fields to empire. Augustine, later in this era, read the fourth Eclogue in the light of Christian faith. Much later, English poets of the 1700s wrote whole “georgics” of their own, and writers on country life kept returning to Virgil’s question of how working the land shapes a person.

questions: Which weather signs have you noticed yourself? Do any of Virgil’s work where you live?
Virgil says farmers are fortunate “did they know their own happiness.” Are there good things in your own life you might not notice?
Is hard work something to escape, or something that makes us better? Can it be both?
In the first Eclogue one neighbor keeps his farm and the other loses his. How should the lucky one treat the other?
Bees share their work and their food. What jobs in your home are shared, and what would happen if no one did them?
